title: Muay Thai in Thailand: which visa do you need to train?
summary: Coming to Thailand to train Muay Thai? For a short camp stay the visa exemption or a tourist visa may be enough. For months of training, the Destination Thailand Visa (DTV) and the Non-Immigrant ED visa are the two real options. Here is how each works, what it costs, and how to pick a camp.
seoTitle: Muay Thai Visa Guide: DTV, ED Visa or Exemption?
seoDescription: Training Muay Thai in Thailand? Compare the visa exemption, tourist visa, DTV soft power route and ED visa, with costs, camp letters and tips for Bangkok, Phuket, Chiang Mai, Samui and Pattaya.

sections.heading: Pick your visa by how long you'll train
paragraphs: The right visa depends mostly on how long you want to stay. A short training holiday needs very little paperwork. A season of fight camps needs a proper long-stay visa, arranged before you fly.
list: Up to about a month: the visa exemption, if your passport qualifies.
One to three months: a Tourist Visa (TR), which gives 60 days and can usually be extended once by 30 days at an immigration office.
Three months to a year or more, coming back often: the Destination Thailand Visa (DTV) under its Muay Thai "soft power" track.
Three to twelve months of structured study at one school: a Non-Immigrant ED (education) visa sponsored by a licensed school.

sections.heading: When the visa exemption is enough
paragraphs: From 15 September 2026, citizens of 54 countries and territories, including the UK, the US, Australia, Canada and most of the EU, can enter without a visa for up to 30 days for tourism. Anyone who entered on the old 60-day exemption before that date keeps the stay they were given.

A few weeks of classes at a gym as part of a holiday is how many people start. If you plan to train for longer, fight on cards, or keep coming back, get the right visa rather than relying on repeated exemption entries. Immigration officers can refuse entry to people who look like they are living in Thailand on exemptions, and land-border entries are limited.
Whatever you enter on, fill in the free Thailand Digital Arrival Card (TDAC) at tdac.immigration.go.th within three days before you arrive.

sections.heading: The DTV: the Muay Thai "soft power" track
paragraphs: The Destination Thailand Visa (DTV) is a five-year, multiple-entry visa. Each entry gives you up to 180 days, and you can extend once by up to another 180 days at an immigration office. Besides remote workers, it covers people joining Thai "soft power" activities, and Muay Thai training is the best-known of these.
The government fee is 10,000 THB, charged in local currency by your embassy. You apply online at thaievisa.go.th to the embassy for the country where you live.
list: An acceptance or enrolment letter from the camp, confirming your course and its dates. Ask for it on the camp's letterhead, signed, with contact details.
The camp's business registration or licence, showing it is a legally registered business. Good camps have a ready-made DTV pack.
Bank statements for the last 3 months with a closing balance of at least 500,000 THB (or the same amount in your own currency).
Passport biodata page and a recent photo.

Proof that you live in the country where you apply. Since 31 August 2026 embassies are reported to want proof of permanent residence, not a hotel booking, and a criminal-record certificate issued within the last six months. Check your embassy's DTV page.
Some embassies ask for more, such as income slips or proof of accommodation. Always follow your embassy's own checklist.

sections.heading: The ED visa from a sponsoring school
paragraphs: The Non-Immigrant ED visa is a study visa. A school licensed to teach Muay Thai, and approved by the relevant Thai authority, sponsors you and sends you the paperwork for your embassy application. It suits people who want a long, structured course at one school and would struggle to show 500,000 THB in savings.

The embassy fee is usually about 2,000 THB for a single entry, charged in local currency (the embassy in Washington, D.C. lists USD 80). The visa gives an entry of up to 90 days. You then extend in Thailand, usually 90 days at a time, with a letter from your school each time. The Immigration Bureau charges 1,900 THB per extension.

The ED visa comes with real obligations. You must attend classes, the school reports your attendance, and immigration can check. Signing up only for the visa and not training can lead to refused extensions and future problems at the border.

sections.heading: What each route costs
paragraphs: Government fees are set by Thai authorities; training prices are set by each camp. The training prices below are typical ranges we see, not official figures, and they change often.
list: Visa exemption: no visa fee. You pay only for training and living costs.
Tourist Visa (TR): the visa fee set by your embassy, plus 1,900 THB if you extend in Thailand.
DTV: 10,000 THB visa fee, 1,900 THB for the one in-country extension, and 500,000 THB in savings that you keep, not spend.
ED visa: about 2,000 THB embassy fee, 1,900 THB for each 90-day extension, and the school's course fee for the ED package, often charged for 6 or 12 months up front.
Training: drop-in sessions often cost a few hundred baht; monthly packages at tourist-friendly camps commonly run from around 8,000 to 20,000 THB, more with accommodation or private lessons.

sections.heading: Choosing a camp: Bangkok, Phuket, Chiang Mai, Koh Samui, Pattaya
paragraphs: Pick a camp for the training first, then check it can support your visa. Ask before you pay whether it issues DTV letters or is licensed for ED visas, and ask to see its registration.
list: Bangkok: the home of the famous stadiums (Rajadamnern and Lumpinee). Traditional fighter camps and modern gyms, city prices, heat and traffic.
Phuket: many large, foreigner-friendly camps, especially around Chalong and Soi Ta-Iad. Easy to combine with a beach holiday; living costs are among the highest in Thailand.
Chiang Mai: cooler in the dry season, cheaper to live, and a good mix of traditional and relaxed camps. Also popular with digital nomads.
Koh Samui: smaller island scene with several well-known camps and a slower pace. Flights to the island are relatively expensive.
Pattaya: a mix of serious fighter camps and fitness gyms, close to Bangkok, with lots of cheap accommodation.

sections.heading: Training and visa etiquette
paragraphs: Muay Thai camps are part of Thai culture as much as they are gyms. A little respect goes a long way, both with trainers and with immigration officers.
list: Keep your camp letter, receipts and schedule with you when you enter Thailand and when you apply for an extension. Officers may ask what you are doing.
Stay within your visa's purpose. A DTV or ED visa lets you train, not coach or work at the camp. Teaching classes for pay needs a work permit.
Fighting on stadium cards can involve prize money. Ask the camp and the promoter how this fits your visa before you accept.
Make sure your accommodation files your TM30 address notification (the form landlords and hotels use to report where foreigners stay). Many camp guesthouses do this for you.
Report your address every 90 days (the "90-day report") if you stay that long without leaving Thailand.
At camp: bow when entering the ring, never step over the ropes, don't point your feet at people or at the shrine, and listen to your trainer.

faqs.q: Can I train Muay Thai on a visa exemption?
faqs.a: Yes, for a short training holiday. From 15 September 2026 the exemption gives most eligible nationalities up to 30 days for tourism. For longer or repeated stays, apply for a DTV, ED or tourist visa before you travel.

faqs.q: DTV or ED visa for Muay Thai: which is better?
faqs.a: The DTV gives more freedom: five years of validity, up to 180 days per entry and no attendance reporting, but you need 500,000 THB in savings. The ED visa needs less money but ties you to one school, with 90-day extensions and attendance checks.

faqs.q: Does any gym's letter work for a DTV?
faqs.a: No. The camp must be a registered business, and embassies may ask for its registration documents. Established camps know the process; if a gym has never heard of it, choose another for your visa.

faqs.q: Can I apply for a DTV from inside Thailand?
faqs.a: No. The DTV is applied for online at thaievisa.go.th to the embassy for the country where you live, and you have to be outside Thailand when you apply.

faqs.q: Can I work at the camp in exchange for training?
faqs.a: Not legally without a work permit. Helping out, coaching or working at reception in exchange for free training counts as work in Thailand.
